evidence: Abstract, Secs.3.3-4 (pp.1,3-4): SHAP attribution drift under FGSM/PGD perturbations on tabular phishing and UNSW-NB15 data
problem: Adversarial perturbations degrade both the accuracy and the interpretability of cybersecurity classifiers.
method: Neural classifiers attacked with L-infinity FGSM and PGD; Robustness Index (area under the accuracy-perturbation curve); gradient-based feature sensitivity; SHAP attribution drift defined as the mean absolute change in SHAP values between clean and perturbed inputs (Eq.6) on 256 test samples; FGSM adversarial-training ablation (eps = 0.05).
data: Phishing Websites (11,000 URLs, 30 features) and UNSW-NB15 (175,000 flows, 42 features), both from Kaggle (p.3).
evaluation: Accuracy vs eps; Robustness Index; per-feature mean absolute SHAP drift; no statistical tests.
findings: Features with high gradient sensitivity also showed the largest SHAP drift, i.e. robustness and interpretability degrade together; adversarial training raised the Robustness Index by up to 9% while keeping clean accuracy (abstract; Sec.4).
limitations: Authors: neural classifiers only; tree-based models left for future work (p.6). Ours: perturbations are adversarial and change predictions, so explanation drift is confounded with prediction change.
repro: Public Kaggle datasets; fixed seeds (p.4); no code link found.
qa_notes: Q2 architecture details brief; Q4 no explainer comparison; Q6 descriptive plots; Q8 data public, no code; Q10 fixed seed, no repetitions.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Authors: neural classifiers only; tree-based models left for future work (p.6). Ours: perturbations are adversarial and change predictions, so explanation drift is confounded with prediction change.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.1-5 (pp.1-17): survey and taxonomy of LIME variants organised by fidelity, stability and domain challenges (review)
read_from: arXiv:2503.24365 (Semantic Scholar lists the xAI 2025 conference version)
problem: The many LIME adaptations proposed to fix fidelity, stability and applicability problems are hard to navigate.
method: Survey of works that explicitly address LIME limitations or improvements; concept matrix; taxonomy by LIME sub-steps (feature generation, sample generation, attribution, representation) and key issues; continuously updated online overview (pp.4-5).
findings: Stability is one of the main problems that LIME variants target; most variants are evaluated on only a subset of criteria, so it is unclear which is superior (p.16).
limitations: Authors: relevant works may be missed given more than 20,000 citing papers (p.5); LIME only, no comparison with SHAP (p.2). Ours: selection process not reported as counts.
repro: Online overview of LIME variants (Fig.1, p.4).
qa_notes: Review: dataset/baseline/metric/randomness items N/A; Q2 selection criteria described but no counts.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.2-5 (pp.1-9): bootstrap uncertainty intervals for local explanations; simulation plus tabular COMPAS, German Credit and Spambase
read_from: Preprint arXiv:2301.05761v3 (24 Jun 2023, 'under review'; no peer-reviewed version found)
problem: When only a static sample of model inputs and outputs is available, local explanations carry finite-sample uncertainty that current explainers do not quantify.
method: Model-agnostic local explanations built from a fixed input-output sample (local polynomial regression, plug-and-play with other local explainers); non-parametric bootstrap uncertainty intervals for feature-importance scores; compared with naive regression confidence intervals and BayesLIME.
data: Simulated ground-truth function; COMPAS and German Credit with random forests; Spambase with a SAINT neural network (p.8).
evaluation: Average interval width and empirical coverage probability in simulation; visual summaries on real data.
findings: Bootstrap intervals gave a better width-coverage trade-off than naive intervals and higher coverage than BayesLIME without model access (pp.1,8).
limitations: Authors: building local models without model access is hard for image data (p.9). Ours: finite-sample uncertainty rather than input perturbation; preprint.
qa_notes: Q6 real-data results visual only; Q7 brief; Q10 simulation over parameter grid.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.2 and 5 (pp.1,3,12-14): stability (30 seeded runs) and robustness (30 resampled refits) of Calibrated Explanations on 25 tabular datasets
read_from: arXiv:2305.02305 version (Semantic Scholar lists Expert Systems with Applications)
problem: Local feature-importance explanations are unstable and distorted by poorly calibrated models, and feature-importance uncertainty is rarely reported.
method: Calibrated Explanations (CE): Venn-Abers calibration plus uncertainty intervals for each feature weight; factual and counterfactual rule-based feature weights; uses LIME's discretiser; random forest and XGBoost.
data: 25 public binary classification datasets from UCI and PROMISE (p.12).
evaluation: Variance of feature weights over 30 explanations with only the seed changed (stability) and over 30 resampled refits (robustness); 20 stratified test instances.
findings: CE was stable by construction (minute variation from seeds); robustness variance was low but clearly larger than stability variance (p.14).
limitations: Authors: future work on user studies and image/text data (p.15). Ours: no direct stability comparison with LIME or SHAP in the experiments read; robustness tested by resampling, not input perturbation.
qa_notes: Q4 no competing explainer in stability tests; Q5 variance only; Q7 brief; Q10 30 runs per dataset.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-9): explainer astuteness (probabilistic Lipschitzness) for SHAP, RISE and CXPlain on simulated and UCI tabular data (plus MNIST)
read_from: arXiv:2206.12481 version of the AISTATS 2024 paper (PMLR 238)
problem: Explainers should give similar explanations for similar inputs, yet small input changes can shift explanations.
method: Defines explainer astuteness and proves lower bounds linking it to the predictor's probabilistic Lipschitzness for SHAP, RISE and CXPlain; four classifiers per dataset; 20 explainer runs.
data: Simulated Orange Skin, Nonlinear Additive and Switch; UCI Rice and Telescope; MNIST (p.7).
evaluation: Empirical astuteness against the classifiers' estimated Lipschitz constants; comparison across explainers.
findings: Smoother (lower-Lipschitz) predictors gave more astute explanations; RISE was least and CXPlain most astute on the evaluated data (pp.8-9).
limitations: Authors: bound could be tightened; tabular LIME with discretisation is not astute by this definition; robustness can conflict with correctness (p.9).
repro: Public explainer implementations and OpenXAI used (pp.7-8); no paper-specific code link found.
qa_notes: Q8 libraries public, no paper code; Q10 20 explainer runs.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-9): GPEC uncertainty for KernelSHAP/BayesSHAP/BayesLIME explanations on tabular Census, Online Shoppers and German Credit (plus images)
read_from: arXiv:2210.02419 version of the AISTATS 2024 paper (PMLR 238)
problem: Local explanations near complex decision boundaries are brittle and their uncertainty is not quantified.
method: Gaussian Process Explanation UnCertainty (GPEC): GP regression over explanations with a decision-boundary-aware geodesic kernel, combining boundary complexity with function-approximation uncertainty; KernelSHAP by default.
data: Three tabular datasets (Census, Online Shoppers, German Credit), synthetic data and image datasets (p.6).
evaluation: Comparison with BayesSHAP, BayesLIME, CXPlain and a naive GP; capture of boundary complexity; ablation; hyperparameter and sample-size sensitivity (appendix).
findings: GPEC uncertainty grew with decision-boundary complexity and gave better insight into explanation reliability than existing methods (abstract; Sec.5).
limitations: Authors: depends on decision-boundary estimation, trading computation time against accuracy (p.9).
qa_notes: Q5 uncertainty estimate rather than a stability metric; Q6 largely visual comparisons; Q10 seeds not reported in sections read.

evidence: Abstract and LIME benchmark section (pp.1,23-24): toolkit paper; LIME stability (VSI/CSI) is one of several secondary benchmarks
Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-9): BayesLIME/BayesSHAP credible intervals and local-Lipschitz stability on tabular COMPAS and German Credit (plus images)
read_from: arXiv:2008.05030 version of the NeurIPS 2021 paper
problem: LIME and KernelSHAP explanations are inconsistent and unstable, give no measure of their reliability and need hyper-parameter tuning.
method: Bayesian versions of LIME and KernelSHAP that return credible intervals for feature importances; 'perturbations-to-go' estimate of the samples needed for a target certainty; focused sampling of perturbations.
data: COMPAS, German Credit, ImageNet and MNIST (p.2).
evaluation: Calibration of credible intervals; stability by local Lipschitz estimate (Eq.12) with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (pp.8-9).
findings: BayesLIME and BayesSHAP were significantly more stable than LIME and SHAP (about 53% on average, p < 0.01), except BayesSHAP on German Credit (p.9).
limitations: Authors: relies on local linear approximation; still vulnerable to sampling-based attacks if LIME/SHAP sampling is kept (Conclusion).
repro: Paper first-page footnote links author project page dylanslacks.website/reliable/index.html, which links code at github.com/dylan-slack/Modeling-Uncertainty-Local-Explainability; public benchmark datasets used.
qa_notes: Q10 repeated sampling with significance tests.; Q8: Author project page links public code and benchmark data; availability checked, experiments not reproduced.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.2-6 (pp.1-4): robustness of LIME to the adversarial scaffolding attack using CTGAN sampling on tabular COMPAS and two other datasets
read_from: arXiv:2006.12302v3 version of the AdvML '20 (KDD workshop) paper
problem: LIME's Gaussian sampling creates off-manifold samples that an adversary can exploit to hide biased behaviour.
method: CTGAN-based locality sampling inside LIME (CTGAN-LIME) vs default LIME; random-forest black box; top-k detection of the hidden sensitive feature.
data: Three real-world tabular datasets including COMPAS and Communities and Crime (pp.1-4).
evaluation: Accuracy of detecting the biased feature among the top-k explanation features.
findings: CTGAN-LIME detected the hidden biased behaviour more accurately than LIME across three datasets, up to 99.94% top-1 accuracy in some cases (abstract).
limitations: Ours: 5-page workshop paper; adversarial robustness rather than benign stability; no repetitions reported.
qa_notes: Q2/Q3 brief; Q5 detection accuracy only; Q6 small experiments; Q10 no repetitions.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Ours: 5-page workshop paper; adversarial robustness rather than benign stability; no repetitions reported.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-6): scaffolding attack hides biased classifiers from LIME and SHAP on tabular COMPAS, Communities and Crime and German Credit
read_from: arXiv:1911.02508 version of the AIES 2020 paper (doi 10.1145/3375627.3375830)
problem: Perturbation-based explainers can be fooled because their synthetic samples lie off the data manifold.
method: Scaffolded classifier with an out-of-distribution detector: biased model on real data, innocuous model on LIME/SHAP perturbations.
data: COMPAS, Communities and Crime, German Credit (p.2).
evaluation: Share of explanations in which the sensitive feature appears at each rank; OOD-detector fidelity.
findings: LIME and SHAP explanations of the biased classifiers did not flag the sensitive attribute; LIME was more vulnerable than SHAP (abstract; Conclusion).
limitations: Authors: other explainer classes left for future work (p.7). Ours: adversarial manipulation, not benign perturbation stability.
qa_notes: Q5 rank-share outcome; Q7 brief; Q9 discrimination and fairwashing discussed; Q10 repetitions not reported.; Q9: Section 3 (Building Adversarial Classifiers) explicitly explains how discriminatory predictions can be hidden behind apparently fair LIME/SHAP explanations; this addresses fairwashing risk, not an ethics-approval claim.

evidence: Abstract and Sec.2.3 (pp.1-4): aims are interaction-induced infidelity and the iBreakDown method; uncertainty from variable order is a secondary illustration
Abstract, Secs.3-4 (pp.1-4): three sources of uncertainty in LIME on synthetic tree data, COMPAS (tabular) and 20 Newsgroups (text)
read_from: arXiv:1904.12991v2 (ICML 2019 AI for Social Good workshop paper)
problem: LIME explanations contain uncertainty that can undermine users' trust in predictions.
method: Repeated LIME runs (100 per point) on a random forest trained on synthetic tree-generated data; varying sample size and sampling proximity; text and COMPAS case studies.
data: Synthetic 8- and 4-feature tree-generated data; 20 Newsgroups; COMPAS (pp.2-6).
evaluation: Empirical selection probability of features across repeated LIME runs.
findings: Sampling randomness, the sample-size and proximity settings, and varying model credibility across points all create uncertainty; LIME did not always select the locally important features (Fig.2, p.3).
limitations: Ours: short workshop paper; descriptive evidence; no stability index.
qa_notes: Q3 data preprocessing brief; Q4 no baseline; Q5 selection probability only; Q6 descriptive; Q8 none; Q10 100 repeated runs.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Ours: short workshop paper; descriptive evidence; no stability index.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.2-3 (pp.1-4): local Lipschitz robustness of LIME and SHAP on UCI tabular data and COMPAS (plus images)
read_from: arXiv:1806.08049 (ICML 2018 Workshop on Human Interpretability in Machine Learning)
problem: Robustness (similar inputs should get similar explanations) is a key desideratum of interpretability but is not measured.
method: Local Lipschitz estimate of explanation change within an eps-ball (continuous optimisation; discrete sample-based version for categorical data); LIME, SHAP and gradient-based methods.
data: UCI datasets (e.g., Boston) and COMPAS with black-box classifiers; MNIST and ImageNet for gradient methods (p.3).
evaluation: Local Lipschitz estimates aggregated over test points.
findings: Current methods, including LIME and SHAP, performed poorly on the robustness metrics; very close points received considerably different explanations (abstract; Sec.3).
limitations: Authors: robustness may conflict with other goals; enforcing robustness proposed as future work (Sec.4). Ours: short workshop paper.
repro: Uses author implementations of LIME and SHAP and DeepExplain (p.3); no paper code link.
qa_notes: Q3 dataset details brief; Q6 small-scale; Q8 libraries only; Q10 sampling described, no repeated seeds.; Q7=0.5: original appraisal retained; supporting extracted limitations: Authors: robustness may conflict with other goals; enforcing robustness proposed as future work (Sec.4). Ours: short workshop paper.
